hook.line: At the Medellín terminal, fifty suitcases come off the bus and none of them is Tomás's. A man holds one up and asks him. You can't answer with *mi*: it needs a thing after it. You need mine.
hook.es:
¿Esta maleta es suya?
No, la mía es la roja.
hook.en:
Is this suitcase yours? (formal)
No, mine is the red one.

rule:
*mi*, *tu* and *su* only work in front of a thing. The long forms work everywhere else:
after *es* or *son*: *Es mía.* It's mine.
after the thing: *un amigo mío*, a friend of mine.
with *el* or *la* and no thing: *la mía*, mine.

The set:
*mío*: mine
*tuyo*: yours (to a friend)
*suyo*: his, hers, theirs, yours (formal)
*nuestro*: ours

They match the thing, not the owner, like any adjective: *mío*, *mía*, *míos*, *mías*. Tomás says *la maleta es mía* because *maleta* is a *la* word, even though he's a man.

English says a friend of mine. Spanish needs no extra word: *un amigo mío*.

And when someone asks whose, one word does it: *Mía.*
smallPrint: Teachers call these stressed possessives (or tonic possessives), as opposed to the short ones, *mi*, *tu*, *su*, that go in front.

options: That phone is mine, isn't it?
That phone is yours, isn't it?
That phone is ours, isn't it?

readAndPick.es: Las mías están en el bus.
Una prima mía vive en Cali.
options: A cousin of mine lives in Cali.
A cousin of yours lives in Cali.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *mío* or *mía* and type the whole sentence: ¿La maleta? Es ___.
yourTurn.why: *Maleta* is a *la* word, so mine is *mía*, whoever owns it.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *tuyo* or *tuyos* and type the whole sentence: ¿Estos tiquetes son ___?
Choose *mía* or *la mía* and type the whole sentence: Tu maleta es negra y ___ es azul.
yourTurn.answer: Tu maleta es negra y la mía es azul.
yourTurn.why: Standing in for the suitcase, mine needs its *la*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: A friend of mine lives in Santa Marta.
yourTurn.answer: Un amigo mío vive en Santa Marta.
yourTurn.why: Of mine is just *mío* after the noun, no *de*.

yourTurn.prompt: Ask a stranger (*usted*): Is this suitcase yours?
yourTurn.why: Yours to *usted* is *suyo*, and *maleta* makes it *suya*.

yourTurn.prompt: Someone asks *¿De quién es esta maleta?* It's yours. Answer in one word.
yourTurn.why: To a whose question, the long form can stand alone, no *la*.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it plural: *Esta llave es mía.*
yourTurn.why: Everything that points at the keys goes plural, *mías* too.

pitfalls.why: Almost. *Mi* always needs a thing after it; on its own, mine is *mío*.

pitfalls.wrong: Un amigo de mí vive en Cali.
pitfalls.right: Un amigo mío vive en Cali.
pitfalls.why: Spanish has no of me for owning: put *mío* after the noun.
It matches the suitcase, a *la* word, not the person who owns it.

pitfalls.wrong: Mi maleta es azul y tuya es negra.
pitfalls.right: Mi maleta es azul y la tuya es negra.
pitfalls.why: Standing in for a thing, yours needs *la* or *el* in front.

personal: Compare something of yours with a friend's: *Mi celular es… y el tuyo es…* Then name a friend of yours who lives far away: *Un amigo mío vive en…*
